From what I've read, the problem with that is time. For a four digit numerical PIN, that's 10,000 combinations to brute force it. If you have to copy gigs of data to the phone every few tries, it's going to take you years to crack it.

On newer phones this won't work at all because the encryption is all done inside a chip called the Secure Enclave. The keys are stored inside the chip in on-die memory, encrypted with a key that's automatically generated from the entered passcode. Wrong passcode means wrong generated key which means wrongly decrypted master encryption key. When you type in your passcode, the phone sends it to this chip which generates the passcode key and tries to decrypt the master key. It then checks the decrypted master key to see if it works, and if it doesn't, it decrements the on-chip counter. When the counter hits zero, it wipes the encrypted key and all the data on the phone is so much random noise.

To read even the encrypted master key, you'd have to shave the top off the chip and extract the data directly from the on-die memory. This is virtually impossible to do without destroying the data in the process, before you can read it.
